Adult Freckled madtom (Noturus nocturnus) attain a maximum recorded total length of 16.2 centimeters [Li = 16.2 centimeters], a modest size characteristic of the cryptic, benthic madtom clade inhabiting rocky riffles of the eastern United States. Maturation in this species is preceded by a distinct juvenile growth phase, and field surveys indicate that puberty is attained at a total length of 9.2 centimeters [Lp = 9.2 centimeters], a measurement that corresponds to a standard length of approximately 7.8 centimeters. At this body size, individuals have undergone the transition from the fingerling stage to a sub-adult condition and begin to exhibit the early morphological and physiological signs of reproductive activation. The adult body mass associated with this length, derived from length-weight regressions, is approximately 5.6 grams [Wwp = approximately 5.6 grams]. This relatively low mass at maturity reflects the species’ overall diminutive body plan and suggests that substantial somatic growth remains possible after the onset of gonadal development. In comparative terms, the pubertal length is just over half the species’ ultimate total length, a proportion that is consistent with an iteroparous life history where reproduction is distributed across multiple adult years.

Egg diameter in the Freckled madtom is approximately 2.3 millimeters, a dimension that directly determines the mass of the newly hatched larva. Upon chorion rupture, the emerging yolk-sac larva, still lecithotrophic and non-feeding, has an estimated wet weight of 0.0064 grams [Wwb = 0.0064 grams]. This extreme mass at birth, less than one hundredth of a gram, is typical of small-bodied ictalurids that produce numerous, small ova and whose offspring depend entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves during the initial days post-hatching. The prolarva remains attached to its substantial yolk sac, absorbing nutrients progressively until the mouth opens and exogenous feeding commences. This period of endotrophic nutrition represents a critical bottleneck in the early life cycle, as the survival of the alevin hinges on the yolk supply lasting until the small prey items required for first feeding are successfully captured. After the trophic switch is achieved, the now exogenously feeding larva enters a pelagic larval phase characterized by rapid mass increase and gradual fin ray ossification. The postpartum mass sets the initial condition for this entire growth trajectory.

The ultimate wet weight of the species, attained by fully grown, reproductively active adults, is estimated at 32.3 grams [Wwi = 32.3 grams]. This asymptotic mass is reached by the largest individuals and reflects the upper boundary of the length-weight relationship derived from mature teleosts. In ecological terms, this body mass is modest even among conspecific ictalurids, placing the Freckled madtom among the smaller members of the genus Noturus. The allometric scaling of mass with length in this species results in a body shape that is relatively elongate, consistent with a life spent sheltering beneath cobble and gravel in shallow stream reaches. Although individuals continue to add somatic tissue as they age, the growth rate decelerates markedly after the attainment of sexual maturity, with most additional mass gain occurring between puberty and the later part of the lifespan. This pattern of asymptotic growth is typical for a teleost with an indeterminate, albeit slowing, growth trajectory. Large, old females nearing their ultimate body mass contribute disproportionately to the reproductive output of the population.

Under constant thermal conditions at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], female Freckled madtom of approximately 7.5 centimeters standard length produce roughly 116 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = roughly 116 eggs per spawning event] and complete approximately one spawning event per year [F_R_i = approximately one spawning event per year]. This annual reproductive output represents the highest recorded rate for this species under controlled laboratory conditions, reflecting the number of propagules a mature female can generate across a single spawning season. The reproductive strategy of the Freckled madtom is iteroparous: females spawn repeatedly over multiple breeding seasons rather than investing in a single, massive clutch. In the wild, the actual number of eggs laid per spawning event may vary with local resource availability, female condition, and population density. Temperature plays a crucial role in mediating the rate of vitellogenesis and the interval between clutches, with the 18 °C [T = 18 °C] regime representing an optimal thermal window for sustained gamete production and oocyte maturation. At temperatures below this threshold, reproductive rates decline substantially.

Experimental data and mark-recapture studies indicate that the maximum lifespan of the Freckled madtom under natural environmental conditions is approximately 4 years [am = approximately 4 years] when maintained at a water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This longevity is relatively short compared to larger ictalurids, but it is not unusual for a small-bodied, riffle-dwelling species that experiences periodic high-mortality events such as spates and droughts. The lifespan appears to be bounded by intrinsic physiological limits, with the oldest individuals typically exhibiting signs of reproductive senescence and a decline in body condition before natural mortality occurs. The interplay between this finite lifespan and the annual fecundity described earlier yields a lifetime reproductive output that is heavily influenced by the number of successful spawning events an individual can complete before senescent death. For a female that reaches the maximum longevity of 4 years and reproduces each year at the highest recorded rate, total lifetime fecundity could approach several hundred eggs, though most wild individuals likely produce fewer due to environmental stochasticity. This comparatively fast life history, with early maturity, a moderate growth rate, and a short adult phase, is well-adapted to the dynamic, disturbance-prone stream habitats this species occupies.
